intro: Advice from SME members and the faculty we talk to, for students in manufacturing, quality and engineering technology. Have a tip? Post it in the Discord and an officer will add it here.

tips.title: The short answer: what to get as a manufacturing student
points: 1. Learn the tools in class first. Lean Manufacturing and Six Sigma (Tech 145) and QA/QC (Tech 31) cover most of a Green Belt's material: DMAIC, SIPOC, control charts, Gage R&R, root cause.
2. If you want a credential before you graduate, get a Green Belt from an exam-based body. IASSC is open to students: one proctored exam, no prerequisites, about $350.
3. Put a real project with a number next to it. A club or class project ("cut changeover time 30%") is worth more to a hiring manager than the belt itself.
4. After you are hired, get the next belt through your employer's program or ASQ, once you have the work experience they require.

tips.title: Why Green and not Black
points: Belts go White, Yellow, Green, Black, then Master Black Belt. A Green Belt matches what a new grad actually does: help on improvement projects and run the tools.

A Black Belt says you have led improvement projects. Faculty we talked to, including one with years at Toyota, say a new grad with a Black Belt reads as overstated to experienced engineers. Engineers online say the same thing.
A Black Belt is still a real, recognized credential. It is just weak without led projects behind it, so it does not help as much as the name suggests.

tips.title: Who issues it matters more than the color
points: There is no single official Six Sigma body, so belts from different issuers are not equal. Quality engineers look at who issued it.
ASQ (CSSGB, CSSBB): the best-known in quality. The Green Belt requires 3 years of full-time work experience, so it is a goal for after graduation.
IASSC: exam-only, no prerequisites, proctored and closed book. The strongest belt a student can earn.

Online-only providers (for example MSI, the Management and Strategy Institute): online exam plus a project simulation, no real project required even for Black Belt, often discounted on deal sites. Real but light; it is worth about what it costs.
Employer-issued belts with a project on their own line carry the most weight with that employer and its industry.

tips.title: Already have a belt? How to show it
points: Keep it. Put it in a Certifications section near the bottom of your resume, not at the top or in your headline. Faculty here give the same advice even for students holding a Black Belt.
Write the issuer and year, for example "Lean Six Sigma Green Belt, IASSC, 2026".
Be ready to talk through one project where you used the tools. That is what interviewers will ask about.

tips.title: Tech 31 and Tech 145 overlap: study them together
points: QA/QC (Tech 31) and Lean Manufacturing and Six Sigma (Tech 145) share a lot: DMAIC, SIPOC, voice of the customer, CTQs, defects vs nonconformities, Gage R&R. Learning a tool once for both classes saves time.
Know the difference in focus: Lean goes after waste (overproduction is the big one), Six Sigma goes after variation and defects.

tips.title: TI-84 stats tricks
points: For infinity in normalcdf, type 1E99 with the EE key (2nd then comma). Do not use the ^ key; it gives a wrong answer.
Use Sx, not σx, when you have a sample.
Turn on DiagnosticOn (catalog) so LinReg shows r and r².

tips.title: Go on the tours and do a project
points: Company tours (Tesla, Rigetti this year) are the easiest way to see a real line and meet engineers. Bring questions and ask for a contact.
Join a club project like Spartan Signs or Ain't No Waymo. It gives you resume bullets with real numbers before your senior project starts.

tips.title: Watch your units if you change majors
points: Past 180 units, financial aid can place an Excessive Unit hold. If that happens, file a SAP appeal with a graduation plan early, before the semester starts. Check with Financial Aid for the current rules.
